name: Cajun spice rub
about: A bold, earthy, peppery blend from Louisiana built on paprika, garlic, onion, herbs and a kick of cayenne. It gives meat and fish a deep red, savoury, slightly smoky crust with warmth that builds rather than burns. Classic for blackened fish or chicken, and great shaken over corn, potatoes or prawns.

name: Kansas City sweet & smoky BBQ rub
about: The sweet end of American barbecue: brown sugar and paprika lead, with chilli, garlic and pepper behind. The sugar caramelises into a sticky, dark, sweet-smoky bark, so it suits long, low cooks of ribs, pork shoulder and chicken, and pairs naturally with a tomatoey BBQ sauce.

name: Texas SPG rub (salt, pepper, garlic)
about: Salt, pepper, garlic – the minimalist Texas approach that lets the meat and smoke do the talking. The result is savoury and peppery with a coarse, crunchy crust rather than a sweet one. Ideal for brisket and steak, and an easy everyday seasoning for anything grilled.

name: Montreal steak seasoning
about: A coarse, punchy steakhouse seasoning from Montreal's delis: cracked pepper, coriander seed, garlic, dill seed and chilli flakes. Expect a bold, peppery, slightly herby, crunchy crust with a mild tingle. Made for steaks and burgers but just as good on roast potatoes or mushrooms.

name: All-purpose pork rub with pan butter
about: A mild, savoury, family-friendly rub of the sweet-paprika-garlic-and-herb kind, finished with butter in the pan. It gives pork and chicken a golden, gently sweet, buttery crust without heat. A safe crowd-pleaser with roast veg and greens.

name: Ras el hanout
about: Moroccan for "head of the shop" – the spice merchant's best blend, so every version differs. Warm and fragrant rather than hot: cumin, coriander, cinnamon, ginger and often rose or cardamom, giving a sweet-savoury, perfumed depth. Superb with lamb, tagines and roasted roots, squash or cauliflower, and lovely with dried fruit.

name: Berbere spice mix
about: Ethiopia's signature spice mix: dried chilli with warm spices like fenugreek, cardamom and allspice. Deep brick-red, smoky, earthy and genuinely hot, with a slightly sweet, bitter-spice complexity. The backbone of Ethiopian stews (wats) with chicken, lentils or beans, and a great rub for roast meat or veg.

name: Dukkah
about: An Egyptian mix of toasted nuts and seeds (typically hazelnuts, sesame, coriander and cumin). It's crunchy, nutty and gently aromatic rather than spicy. Traditionally eaten by dipping bread in oil then dukkah; also great as a crust on lamb or fish, or scattered over eggs, roast veg and salads for texture.

name: Za'atar
about: Both a wild herb and the Levantine blend made from it: thyme/oregano-like herbs with tangy, lemony sumac and toasted sesame. Earthy, herbal and sour-bright with a nutty finish. Classic on flatbread with olive oil, and brilliant on roast chicken, eggs, labneh, tomatoes or potatoes.

name: Tandoori dry rub
about: The dry version of tandoori seasoning: paprika or Kashmiri chilli for colour, plus cumin, coriander, garam masala and ginger. Warm, smoky and earthy with moderate heat and that signature red colour. Good when you want tandoori flavour without a yoghurt marinade – on chicken, fish, paneer or cauliflower.

name: Chinese five-spice
about: A Chinese blend that aims to balance all five flavours: star anise, cloves, cinnamon, Sichuan pepper and fennel. Sweet, warm and liquorice-scented with a faint numbing tingle. A little goes a long way; it's classic with fatty meats like pork belly and duck, and in braises and stir-fries.

name: Shichimi togarashi
about: Japanese "seven-flavour chilli": chilli with citrus peel, sesame, seaweed and sanshō pepper. Bright, citrusy and nutty with a sharp, tingly heat. Used as a table sprinkle rather than a marinade – over noodles, udon, rice bowls, grilled chicken (yakitori) and fish.

name: Herbes de Provence
about: A dried herb blend from southern France: thyme, rosemary, savory and oregano, sometimes with lavender. Resinous, woody and floral with no heat – the smell of the Mediterranean hillside. Natural with roast chicken, lamb and ratatouille-type veg like tomatoes, courgette and aubergine.

name: Jamaican jerk marinade
about: Jamaica's fiery, aromatic marinade built on scotch bonnet chillies, allspice and thyme, with spring onion, garlic and ginger. Intensely hot, fruity, herbal and warmly spiced, and traditionally cooked over smoky wood. Best on chicken and pork; cool it down with rice and peas or something sweet like grilled corn or pineapple.

name: Bulgogi marinade
about: Korean "fire meat": a soy-based marinade sweetened with sugar and often grated pear, plus garlic, sesame and spring onion. Sweet, savoury and nutty, and the fruit helps tenderise thin slices of beef. Cooks quickly to caramelised edges; eat with rice, lettuce wraps and kimchi.

name: Saikyo-style miso marinade
about: A Kyoto style using sweet white (Saikyo) miso with sake and mirin. Mellow, sweet, savoury (umami) and a little funky; it seasons deeply and caramelises to a glossy, slightly charred glaze. Famous on black cod and salmon, and excellent on aubergine and tofu.

name: Greek lemon, garlic & oregano marinade
about: The taste of a Greek taverna: lemon juice, garlic, dried oregano and olive oil. Bright, tangy, herbal and fresh with no heat. Superb on lamb chops, souvlaki and chicken, and it runs straight into the classic lemon potatoes. Very acidic, so don't leave fish in it long.

name: Piri-piri marinade & glaze
about: Portuguese-African chilli sauce made from small, hot bird's-eye (piri-piri) chillies with garlic, citrus or vinegar and oil. Hot, sharp, tangy and garlicky – think Nando's. Used both to marinate and to baste, it's best known on grilled chicken and prawns, with chips or rice.

name: Tandoori yoghurt marinade
about: A Punjabi yoghurt marinade with ginger, garlic, lemon and warm spices. The yoghurt tenderises and clings, giving a tangy, smoky, spiced, charred crust with moderate heat. The classic for tandoori chicken, and great with lamb, fish, paneer or cauliflower.

name: Thai satay marinade
about: A Thai-style marinade of coconut milk, turmeric, lemongrass and curry-type spices. Fragrant, mildly sweet and golden-yellow; it keeps skewers juicy and lightly spiced. Served with peanut satay sauce (see Sauces) and a sharp cucumber relish.

name: Vietnamese lemongrass marinade
about: Lemongrass, garlic, shallot, fish sauce and a touch of sugar. Fresh, citrusy-floral, salty-sweet and savoury, and it chars beautifully. Classic on grilled pork for bún (noodle bowls) or broken rice, with fresh herbs and nuoc cham.

name: Filipino adobo (marinade & glaze)
about: The Philippines' national dish is more a style than a single recipe: meat braised in vinegar, soy sauce, garlic, bay and peppercorns, then often crisped. Sharp and tangy, salty and garlicky, mellowing into rich, glossy savouriness. Chicken or pork with plenty of rice to soak up the sauce.

name: Huli huli marinade
about: Hawaiian "turn-turn" chicken, rotated on the grill while basted with a sweet glaze of pineapple, soy, ginger and brown sugar. Sweet, tangy, sticky and savoury, like a fruitier teriyaki. Good for chicken or pork at a barbecue, with rice and grilled pineapple or peppers.

name: Al pastor chilli & pineapple marinade
about: A Mexican taco filling born from Lebanese shawarma: pork marinated in dried chillies, achiote and pineapple, stacked on a vertical spit. Smoky, earthy, mildly hot and tangy-sweet, with a deep red colour. Served in corn tortillas with pineapple, onion and coriander.

name: Cuban mojo marinade
about: Cuba's citrus marinade: sour (Seville) orange or orange and lime juice with lots of garlic, oregano and cumin. Tangy, zesty and heavily garlicky. The classic for slow-roast pork (lechón), also great on chicken or seafood, with rice, black beans and yuca or potatoes.

name: Anticucho marinade
about: Peruvian street-food skewers marinated in ají panca chilli paste, vinegar, cumin and garlic. Smoky, earthy, tangy and moderately hot, with a mild fruity chilli flavour. Traditionally beef heart, but works on steak, chicken or pork, with potatoes and corn.

name: Shish taouk marinade
about: A Lebanese chicken kebab marinade of yoghurt, lemon, garlic and mild spices like paprika. Tangy, garlicky and tender, with a light char. Served in flatbread with toum (garlic sauce), pickles and grilled peppers and tomatoes.

name: Joojeh saffron-yoghurt marinade
about: Iranian chicken kebab marinade of saffron, onion, lemon and yoghurt. Delicately floral, tangy and golden rather than spicy. Traditionally grilled and served with buttery saffron rice and charred tomatoes.

name: Chermoula
about: A North African herb paste of coriander, parsley, garlic, lemon, cumin and paprika. Green, zesty, earthy and gently warm. Especially good with fish and seafood; use it as a marinade or spoon it over as a sauce. Also lovely with chicken, potatoes and roast veg.

name: Diane sauce
about: A retro steakhouse pan sauce of shallots, mushrooms, mustard, Worcestershire sauce and cream, often flambéed with brandy. Rich, savoury, tangy and creamy with a mild mustard bite. Made in the pan after searing steak; also good with pork or chicken and a side of chips or greens.

name: Creamy peppercorn sauce
about: The steak au poivre sauce: crushed peppercorns (black or green) with brandy, stock and cream. Rich and creamy with a warm, aromatic pepper bite. The classic partner for steak and chips, and great with pork, chicken or duck.

name: Béarnaise
about: A French butter sauce (a cousin of hollandaise) flavoured with tarragon, shallot and vinegar. Rich, buttery and velvety, with an aniseed-herbal note and a sharp tang that cuts the richness. The steak-frites classic; also excellent with fish, salmon and eggs.

name: Beurre blanc
about: "White butter" from the Loire: a reduction of wine, vinegar and shallots with lots of butter whisked in. Silky, rich and delicately tangy. Designed for poached or pan-fried fish and shellfish; fine with chicken and greens too.

name: Red wine sauce (jus)
about: A reduction of red wine and stock with shallots and herbs, finished with butter. Deep, savoury, glossy and fruity with a slightly sweet-sour edge. The classic for steak, lamb, duck or a Sunday roast, with mushrooms and mashed potatoes.

name: Chimichurri
about: Argentina's parrilla (grill) sauce: parsley, oregano, garlic, chilli flakes, vinegar and oil. Sharp, fresh, herby and garlicky with a mild kick, it cuts through fatty grilled meat. Made for steak and sausages, and great on grilled veg, chicken or fish.

name: Salsa verde
about: Italy's green sauce of parsley and other soft herbs with capers, anchovies, garlic, mustard and oil. Tangy, salty, briny and fresh. Brightens rich or plain foods alike: boiled meats, lamb, steak, fish, eggs, potatoes and beans. (Not the Mexican tomatillo salsa of the same name.)

name: Gremolata
about: A Milanese topping of chopped parsley, lemon zest and garlic – not a sauce so much as a finishing sprinkle. Very fresh, zesty and pungent. Traditionally scattered on osso buco; it lifts any rich braise, fish, seafood or roast veg.

name: Romesco
about: A Catalan sauce of roasted red peppers, tomatoes, garlic, toasted nuts (almonds or hazelnuts), bread and sherry vinegar. Smoky, nutty, sweet-tangy and thick. Traditionally for grilled calçots (spring onions); great with fish, chicken, lamb, potatoes and grilled veg.

name: Tzatziki
about: A Greek dip of strained yoghurt with cucumber, garlic and dill or mint. Cool, creamy, tangy and refreshing. Tames grilled and spiced meats – souvlaki, lamb, chicken, gyros – and goes with pitta, chips and raw veg.

name: Garlicky harissa
about: A Tunisian chilli paste of roasted red chillies with garlic, caraway, coriander and cumin. Hot, smoky, earthy and garlicky. Stir it into stews and couscous, rub it on lamb or chicken, or mix with yoghurt or mayo to tame it. Also great with eggs (shakshuka) and roast veg.

name: Zhoug
about: A Yemeni hot green sauce of coriander, green chillies, garlic and warm spices like cardamom and cumin. Fiery, bright and herbal. Popular in Israel and the Levant on falafel, shawarma, eggs and grilled meat or fish.

name: Green (coriander-mint) chutney
about: An Indian fresh chutney of coriander and mint with green chilli, lime and sometimes yoghurt. Zingy, fresh, sour and hot. Served with samosas, pakoras, tandoori meats, paneer and chaat, and it wakes up rice and potatoes.

name: Peanut satay sauce
about: A peanut sauce with coconut milk, soy, lime and a little chilli and sugar. Rich, nutty, sweet-salty and creamy, with only mild heat. The dip for satay skewers, and good with noodles, tofu, rice and dressed greens (gado-gado).

name: Nuoc cham
about: Vietnam's all-purpose dipping sauce: fish sauce, lime, sugar, garlic and chilli, thinned with water. Light, sweet, sour, salty and hot all at once. Used for spring rolls, noodle bowls, grilled pork or fish and rice dishes.

name: Nam jim jaew
about: A northeastern Thai dipping sauce of fish sauce, lime, dried chilli flakes and toasted ground rice. Sour, salty, smoky and hot, with a nutty crunch from the rice. The classic partner for grilled meats like crying tiger steak and gai yang chicken, with sticky rice.

name: Ponzu
about: A Japanese citrus-soy sauce: soy sauce with the sharp juice of citrus such as yuzu or sudachi, plus mirin and dashi. Thin, tangy, salty and citrusy with light sweetness and umami. Adds a sweet-sour brightness to fish, sashimi, seared beef (tataki), dumplings and hotpots; also good as a dressing.

name: Teriyaki sauce
about: A Japanese glaze of soy sauce, mirin, sake and sugar reduced to a glossy coating (teri = shine, yaki = grill). Sweet, salty and savoury with a sticky, caramelised finish. Classic on chicken, salmon and beef, served with rice and greens.

name: Mole poblano
about: A famous Mexican sauce from Puebla combining dried chillies, nuts and seeds, spices, dried fruit and a little chocolate. Deep, rich, dark and complex: smoky, sweet, bitter and mildly hot – chocolate adds depth, not dessert flavour. Traditionally served over turkey or chicken with rice.

name: Pico de gallo
about: A fresh Mexican salsa of chopped tomato, onion, coriander, chilli and lime. Crunchy, bright, juicy and fresh with mild heat. Spooned over tacos, grilled meats, fish, eggs and beans, or served with tortilla chips.
